newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania debates emergency rule after rioting.
newsitem.headline: Albania debates emergency rule after rioting.

text.p: Albania's leaders denounced two days of anti-government rioting in which three people died as the work of leftist extremists and urged parliament to back emergency measures on Tuesday to quell it.
The assembly appeared divided on curbing civil liberties in the southern port of Vlore, where protesters pelted riot police with stones on Monday and drove them out of a central square.
Up to 100 people were injured in the clashes.
"Now in Vlore it is calm, but during the day the situation was very, very difficult," Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi told reporters in English after debate in parliament closed late on Monday night.
"Forces of the extreme left were intent on killing hundreds of people and destroying the police station. We want to take extraordinary measures to prevent a deterioriation in Vlore."
Deputies postponed a decision until Tuesday, pending adoption of a law on emergency rule.
Meksi, who has headed the government for five years in what was once Europe's most hardline Stalinist regime, rejected opposition calls to resign.
He told parliament the unrest had nothing to do with protesters' anger at losing their life savings in shady pyramid investment schemes.

"The Albanian state is not prepared for this degree of violence," the ATA news agency quoted him as saying. "I am therefore asking for army intervention, declaration of a state of emergency in Vlore and control on movements in Albania."
Demonstrators blaming right-wing President Sali Berisha for their lost savings left the city centre by early evening.
Thousands of frenzied protesters had pelted police with paving stones scooped up from the street by pensioners.
About 30 officers cornered at a cafe had chairs and tables flung at them from an overhead terrace and were forced to strip off their uniforms.
Protesters and police were then locked in a tense stand-off for hours outside the police station, where clashes first erupted on Sunday evening.

Hospital officials said one demonstrator in the latest fray had died of a bullet wound, a second of a heart attack. Both were to be buried on Tuesday. A Moslem funeral took place on Monday for a third demonstrator who died in the initial clash.
State television showed at length doctors struggling to cope with casualties, some covered in bloodstained bandages, others writhing or lying motionless on hospital beds.

The Health Ministry said 26 people, policemen and protesters, remained in hospital with injuries and 55 were released after treatment. More than 60 policemen were among the injured, including some transferred to a Tirana hospital.
Though dominated by Berisha's supporters, parliament was by no means sure to agree to emergency rule.
"The prime minister's statement is unacceptable," said Sabri Godo of the far-right Republican Party. "I invite deputies to find a political, not military, solution."

Even members associated with Berisha's Democratic Party expressed reservations. Bashkim Kopilku, a former deputy prime minister, said it was time to replace the government with a new administration formed by the ruling party.

The opposition Forum for Democracy alliance renewed its calls for Berisha to appoint a "technocrat government" to tackle the pyramid crisis. Nearly every family in the country of 3.4 million has sunk money into the schemes.
The Forum called a rally in a Tirana stadium on Wednesday. An opposition demonstration in the capital last weekend, banned by authorities, was broken up by riot police with truncheons.
